shape_target: 600-1200 chars per text, multi-sentence paragraphs at production-ingest shape
notes: V3-prod expansion of V2 SCR eval to production shape. Same 4 roles (state_change_report, investigation, observation, preference). Each topic appears exactly twice with different roles to keep the eval balanced. Disjoint from prototypes_v3_production.json by topic and by exact text. Anti-leak (topic disjointness + exact-text disjointness) is enforced at runtime by the few_shot_classifier_v2.py harness.

events.text: Stripe has been the primary payment processor since the 2026-04-15 cutover. The Adyen integration that used to handle 18% of European transactions was decommissioned that week, and refund flows have been rerouted entirely through the Stripe gateway. The platform fee structure was published to the partner portal on 2026-04-12, and customer-facing invoices were updated to reflect the new processor on 2026-04-18. Reconciliation for the legacy Adyen ledger completed on 2026-04-22, and the historical export was archived to the finance data lake. The Stripe SDK version is pinned at v18.4 across services, and the webhook handler fleet has handled the post-cutover traffic with no reported errors for two consecutive weeks. Engineering closed the migration runbook and posted the validation report to the platform-finance space.

Production search has been running on Vespa since the 2026-03-22 release. The legacy Elasticsearch cluster was placed in read-only mode that day and fully shut down on 2026-04-05 after the search-relevance review confirmed parity with the new system. The Vespa index now serves 4.2 billion documents across the public and internal corpora, and the indexer pipeline has been steady at about 220 docs/sec ingest. The historical Elasticsearch snapshot was archived to S3 Glacier, and the cluster's compute reservation was released on 2026-04-08. Internal services calling the search API were updated to the new client library between 2026-03-15 and 2026-03-21, and the deprecation notices were removed from the API docs. The post-cutover search-quality dashboard has been live since the release.

Triton has handled all ML inference traffic since 2026-04-01. The legacy serving fleet that ran on TF Serving was decommissioned that week, and the GPU reservation backing it was released to the shared platform pool. The new Triton fleet has 24 nodes split across three regions, and the autoscaler is configured for a 30-second cold-start budget. Model registry has been updated so that all production checkpoints publish in the Triton-compatible format, and the deprecation of the TF Serving registry path was completed on 2026-04-08. The ml-platform team published the new ops runbook on 2026-04-05, and the post-cutover validation report was approved on 2026-04-10. Internal serving SLOs (p99 latency 80ms, error rate <0.5%) have been met every day since the cutover.

Dual-write of new uploads to S3 and R2 went live on 2026-04-05. The dual-write fan-out is implemented in the storage gateway service and runs on a best-effort basis for R2; failures on the secondary write are logged but do not surface to the user. The historical backfill from S3 to R2 completed on 2026-04-15, and the byte-level reconciliation matched 99.997% of objects. The gateway version was promoted to v3.2.1 on the cutover date, and the prior v3.1 builds were retired the following Monday. Internal teams have been notified that R2 is the secondary tier and should not be used as a source of truth yet. The metrics dashboard now exposes the dual-write success rate, and storage-cost reporting has been split by tier in the finance pipeline since 2026-04-12.

Per-seat enterprise billing went into effect on 2026-04-01. All enterprise contracts in the renewal pipeline were re-papered to the new structure between 2026-03-10 and 2026-03-28, and the customer success team confirmed the migration with each account. The legacy flat-fee billing path is no longer accessible to new accounts, and the seat-counting logic has been wired into the daily reconciliation job. Internal billing dashboards were updated on 2026-03-30 to expose seat utilization per account, and the finance reconciliation runbook now references the new schema. The 12 affected enterprise contracts have been invoiced under the new model, and no disputes have been filed in the first billing cycle. The flat-fee API endpoint has been documented as a deprecated surface in the API reference, and the existing change-control policy governs its removal cadence.

Sift Score has been integrated for chargeback prevention since 2026-04-08. The integration runs in pre-authorization mode and intercepts roughly 2.4% of attempted transactions for additional review. The legacy heuristic rule engine that handled chargeback prevention before Sift was placed in shadow mode on the cutover date; its decisions are logged for parity comparison but no longer block transactions. Sift's confidence threshold has been pinned at 0.85 in line with the risk team's recommendation, and the false-positive rate measured during the first 10 days was 0.3%, within the agreed budget. The chargeback dashboard now tracks Sift's verdicts side-by-side with the legacy engine's. The risk-platform runbook was updated on 2026-04-12, and the integration retrospective is closed.

Segment has handled the analytics pipeline since 2026-03-18 and Snowplow was sunsetted that day. The Snowplow collector fleet was placed in read-only mode and fully shut down by 2026-04-01, with the historical event archive exported to the analytics data lake. The Segment integration covers all client-side and server-side event sources that previously routed through Snowplow, and the schema-registry was repopulated with the new contract. Downstream consumers were updated between 2026-03-10 and 2026-03-17 to read from Segment's destination connectors. Analytics ingest volume has been steady at 2.3 billion events per day since the cutover, and the data-quality team confirmed schema compliance was at 99.6%. The decommissioning runbook is closed and the Snowplow infra was reclaimed.

Datadog APM has been live in production since the renewal on 2026-04-01. The renewal contract bumped the trace ingest budget by 40%, and tail-based sampling rules were re-tuned to take advantage of the headroom. The prior 6.x agent version was rolled forward to 7.52 across the fleet between 2026-03-28 and 2026-03-31, and the upgrade runbook has been archived to the platform-ops space. Monitor definitions have been re-published from the dashboards-as-code repo, and on-call alerts have been routed through the new APM-aware rules since 2026-04-04. The cost dashboard now reflects the renewed contract, and finance has reconciled the first quarterly invoice. The renewal retrospective was closed on 2026-04-12, with no follow-up action items.

The marketing site has run on React Server Components since 2026-04-09. The previous Next.js Pages Router build was placed behind a feature flag for a one-week parity validation and fully retired on 2026-04-16. The new build's bundle size measured 312KB, the marketing team's content authoring runbook was updated to reflect the new component model, and the deployment runbook for the marketing edge has been republished to the platform-frontend space. Internal previews and the staging environment have been on RSC since 2026-03-25, and the production cutover went through without observable errors. The 14 marketing pages affected by the migration were validated against the design-system snapshot and approved by the marketing lead. CDN cache headers were updated on the cutover date.

Aurora has hosted the production cluster since the 2026-04-03 migration. The legacy self-managed Postgres fleet was placed in read-only mode that day and fully shut down on 2026-04-08 after the validation team confirmed application parity. The Aurora cluster is configured for multi-AZ high availability and is sized at db.r7g.4xlarge for the writer, with two readers for the analytical workload. Backup retention was extended to 35 days, and the point-in-time recovery window has been tested per the resilience policy. The data-platform team published the migration runbook to the platform-data space on 2026-04-04, and the post-migration audit closed on 2026-04-15 with no open findings. Internal services have been running against Aurora exclusively for three weeks.

Looking into why search relevance dropped 6% after the index rebuild last week. The metric we track for relevance is the click-through rate on the top-3 results for a fixed traffic-weighted query basket, and the regression appeared the day after the rebuild completed. The current working theory is that the rebuild silently dropped a small number of synonym entries that are heavily weighted by certain query classes, but we have not been able to confirm because the synonym diff log is incomplete. The team is replaying the rebuild in a shadow environment with full audit logging this week, and we will compare the resulting synonym table against the production one. We expect data within a few days. We are also evaluating whether to roll back the rebuild, but no decision has been made yet because the regression is concentrated on long-tail queries and the cost of a rollback is non-trivial.

Diagnosing the increased crash rate on Android 14 devices that we have been seeing since the most recent client release. The crash rate climbed from 0.12% to 0.41% over the past 10 days, and the regression is concentrated on Pixel devices running Android 14 with the most recent security patch. We have ruled out the obvious GPU-driver theory because the same hardware on the prior security patch is unaffected. We are looking at three angles: the new strict-mode enforcement on Android 14, the modified WebView rendering path on the affected devices, and a possible interaction with the in-app survey SDK that we updated this release. The team is collecting symbolicated stack traces from a sample of affected devices and we expect a clearer picture by end of week. No remediation has been chosen yet.

Root-causing the Kafka consumer lag that started this morning across three of our streaming services. The lag spiked to about 12 minutes during the 09:30 to 11:00 window and has been recovering slowly since then. The current working theory is that the partition assignment churned during the consumer-group rebalance triggered by the deploy, but the rebalance log surface is sparse and we cannot confirm without additional instrumentation. The team is enabling the verbose Kafka client logs on a canary consumer this afternoon, and we are pulling the broker-side metrics for the affected partitions. We expect to have data within a few hours. No customer-facing signal has been impacted yet because the affected services are batched downstream, but the recovery time is approaching the SLO budget and we want a real answer before another deploy goes through.

Investigating the spike in S3 GetObject latency p99 over the past three days. The p99 climbed from 18ms to 64ms during the affected windows, and the regression concentrates on the analytics-export prefix where we read large objects in bulk. We have ruled out the obvious cross-region theory because the same prefix on a sibling bucket in the same region shows no regression. The team is looking at three possible causes: the recent change to the lifecycle policy that introduced a new transition rule, an interaction with the access-pattern-based optimizer that AWS rolled out this quarter, and an internal change to our retrieval client that may be issuing badly-shaped range reads. We are running a controlled benchmark against the prefix this afternoon. No conclusion has been reached and no remediation has been chosen.

Examining the email delivery rate dip in the EU region. The rate dropped from 98.4% to 92.1% over the past two weeks for transactional emails routed through SES, and the regression concentrates on Gmail and Outlook recipients in the affected geography. We have not been able to reproduce the issue from internal test accounts. The current working theory is that one of our recent template revisions introduced content that triggers spam scoring on the affected providers, but the SES feedback signal is sparse and we cannot confirm without additional testing. The team is running a controlled A/B between the prior template and the new one starting this week, and we expect data within five days. No customer-facing impact has been formally reported, but the metric is approaching our internal alert threshold.

Root-causing the false-positive spike in our fraud-detection model that started two weeks ago. The false-positive rate jumped from 0.3% to 1.2% during the affected window, and the regression concentrates on first-time customers placing transactions in the 50-200 USD range. We have ruled out the obvious model-drift theory because the model has not been retrained in the past month. We are exploring whether the upstream feature-engineering pipeline silently changed how it computes the velocity feature; one of the dependent services was upgraded around the same time. The team is replaying the affected transactions through both the current and the prior feature-engineering pipeline this week to see whether the outputs differ. We expect data shortly. No remediation has been chosen yet.

Trying to understand why rolling deployments occasionally hang for 8-15 minutes during the post-rollout validation phase. The pattern shows up roughly once every 12 deploys and is not concentrated on any single service. The current working theory is that the readiness probe definition for the affected services has a race with the upstream service-discovery refresh, but we have not been able to reproduce in staging. The team is enabling probe-event tracing on the next round of deploys, and we are pulling the service-discovery client logs for the most recent affected windows. We expect a clearer picture by next week. We are also evaluating whether to set a hard timeout on the validation phase, but no decision has been made yet because the cost of a premature timeout would be a partial rollback.

Diagnosing why nodes drift from their desired pool size during peak hours. The cluster autoscaler is supposed to maintain a 12-node minimum on the platform pool, but we have been observing brief windows where the pool drops to 9 or 10 nodes during the 11:00 to 14:00 PT window. The current working theory is that the spot-instance reclamation on AWS is racing with the autoscaler's replenishment loop, but we cannot confirm because the reclamation events do not surface in our cluster-events log without additional configuration. The team is enabling spot-event capture on a canary node group this week, and we are pulling the autoscaler's decision-log for the past 14 days. We expect data within a few cycles. No remediation has been chosen yet because the impact has been brief.

Looking into the recent uptick in 504 timeouts on the public API. The 504 rate climbed from 0.04% to 0.18% over the past week, concentrated on the payments and orders endpoints during the post-lunch traffic peak. We have not been able to reproduce in internal load tests. The current working theory is that the upstream ALB's idle-timeout setting is interacting with a recent change to the connection-pool sizing on the API client side, but we have not been able to confirm because the ALB's per-connection logs are sparse during the affected windows. The team is enabling enhanced ALB logging this afternoon, and we are pulling the API client metrics for the affected endpoints. We expect data soon. No customer-facing escalations yet, but the trend is approaching the SLO budget.

Root-causing why scheduled jobs occasionally fire twice during the same window. The pattern shows up roughly once every 200 job runs and is not concentrated on any single workflow type. We have ruled out the obvious cron-server-clock-drift theory because the affected jobs are split across schedulers running in different availability zones. The current working theory is that the scheduler's lease-acquisition path has a race when the underlying lock service is briefly unavailable, but we cannot confirm because the lock-service logs do not capture lease attempts that succeed on retry. The team is instrumenting the lease-acquisition path with finer-grained timing this week, and we are pulling the lock-service availability metrics for the affected windows. We expect a clearer picture in a few days. No remediation has been committed yet.

Stripe processing fees increased 0.3% this quarter, traced to a shift in the merchant mix toward higher-risk categories. Total processed volume measured at 4.8 billion USD, up 11% year-over-year, and the average transaction size rose from 84 to 91 USD. Records show that the merchant mix shift was concentrated in the new SMB onboarding cohort that came in during 2026-Q1, with about 1,400 new merchants enrolled. The fee-impact dashboard has tracked the shift since 2026-02-01, and the finance team has been reviewing the data weekly. The chargeback rate on the new cohort measured at 0.07%, slightly above the platform median but within the contractual tolerance. The fee variance has been visible in the partner-finance reconciliation since the start of the quarter, and the data was discussed at the 2026-04-22 finance review.

ML inference latency p95 has held steady at 45ms across all regions for the past 30 days. The p99 measures at 92ms in us-east-1 and 105ms in eu-west-1, both within the SLO budget. Throughput records show 8.2 million inference calls per hour at peak, distributed across 14 production models. GPU utilization measured at 68% mean during business hours, with the autoscaler triggering a scale-up at the 75% threshold approximately 14 times per day. The cold-start metric measured at 2.1 seconds median, within the 3-second budget. The serving-perf dashboard has tracked these numbers since the Triton cutover, and the data was reviewed in the 2026-04-22 ml-platform sync. No regressions have been recorded over the period.

CDN bandwidth usage shows a clear lunchtime spike pattern in EMEA, with peak utilization climbing from 38% off-peak to 71% during the 11:30-13:00 local window. The cache hit rate dropped from 94% to 81% over the past three weeks, with the regression concentrated on the static-asset prefix. Records indicate the regression began on 2026-04-10, two days after the new build pipeline started emitting hashed asset filenames more aggressively. CDN cost reports show a 12% increase in origin-pull bytes in the affected window. The bandwidth-per-region dashboard captures the trend, and the data was discussed in the 2026-04-22 platform-frontend sync. The CDN provider's logs show no error-rate change. The metric has been visible on the platform-edge dashboard since 2026-04-12.

Failed login rate has been stable around 2.1% over the past 30 days, with no notable spikes outside of the 09:00 PT business-hour ramp. JWT verification metrics show p95 latency at 4ms and the verification cache hit rate measured at 97.4%. The OAuth callback path measured at 280ms p95 across the affected providers, slightly slower than the 220ms observed last quarter. Session-token rotation events fired roughly 14 million times per day, with no anomalies in the rotation-success rate. The platform-auth dashboard captures all these numbers, and the data was reviewed in the 2026-04-22 platform-security sync. The most recent quarterly auth-metrics report was published to the platform-security space last week.

Subscription churn dipped to 1.4% from 1.9% last quarter. The improvement is concentrated on the SMB tier, where churn fell from 2.4% to 1.6%, while enterprise churn held flat at 0.3%. Records show that the SMB improvement coincides with the rollout of the in-product upgrade-prompt experience on 2026-02-20. Monthly recurring revenue measured at 22.4 million USD this quarter, up 7.1% from the prior quarter. The billing-platform dashboard captures the churn breakdown by tier, by acquisition channel, and by tenure bucket; the data was reviewed in the 2026-04-15 finance staff sync. The customer success team has tracked the metric weekly since the experience rollout, and no follow-up actions remain open. The dataset for the quarterly board pack was finalized last week.

Recommendation CTR data shows a flat line across personas this week, holding at 4.7% with no notable variation by user segment. The two-tower model has been serving production traffic since 2026-04-12, and the post-cutover performance has been steady. Daily recommendation impressions measured at 184 million, with the average position-of-click holding at 2.3. The cold-start funnel metric, which tracks new-user CTR in the first session, has been stable at 3.1%, slightly below the all-user mean. The recs-platform dashboard captures these numbers per persona and per surface; the data was reviewed in the 2026-04-22 ml-platform sync. The recs team has been monitoring the metric on a daily cadence, and no anomalies have surfaced. The weekly recs-quality report has been clean for three consecutive weeks.

Analytics events ingested per day plateaued at 2.3 billion. The volume has held within a 2% band for the past 14 days, which is the longest stable window we have seen since the Segment cutover. Records show that the dominant source is mobile client events at 58% of volume, followed by server-side at 32% and web client at 10%. The data-quality dashboard reports a schema-compliance rate of 99.6%, in line with the post-cutover steady state. The downstream warehouse ingest measured at a median lag of 4 minutes, well within the 10-minute SLO. The analytics-platform dashboard captures these numbers; the data was reviewed in the 2026-04-22 data-platform staff sync. No follow-up items are open from the most recent review.

Deployment frequency report shows 14 deploys per week median across the platform org. The metric is broken down by service, with the top three services deploying daily and the long-tail services deploying weekly or less. Mean time to recover from a failed deploy measured at 11 minutes, slightly better than the 14-minute baseline from last quarter. Records show that 94% of deploys completed without rollback, and the rollback rate has been stable for the past six weeks. The deploy-perf dashboard captures all these numbers; the data was reviewed in the 2026-04-22 platform-eng sync. The Argo Rollouts canary success rate measured at 99.1% over the affected window. No follow-up items remain from the most recent quarterly deploy-review.

Frontend bundle size measured at 312KB, up 8% from the baseline. The increase is concentrated on the marketing site, where the React Server Components migration added a 24KB runtime delta that has been stable since 2026-04-09. The Lighthouse performance score for the home route holds at 92 on the desktop profile and 78 on the mobile profile, both unchanged since the migration. Records show first-contentful-paint at 1.2 seconds median on desktop and 2.4 seconds on mobile, with the long tail on mobile concentrated in the global south region. The frontend-perf dashboard captures these numbers per route and per device profile, and the data was reviewed in the 2026-04-22 platform-frontend sync. The pre-migration baseline snapshot was preserved for comparison.

API request mix shows mobile clients are now 62% of traffic, up from 54% last quarter. The shift is consistent across the public-facing endpoints, with no single endpoint driving the change. Total request volume measured at 1.4 billion per day, up 9% quarter-over-quarter. The GraphQL surface, live since 2026-03-28, now serves 18% of the public-facing traffic and the migration of internal consumers off REST has been steady. Records show the average GraphQL query depth holds at 4.1, within the platform's 6-deep budget. The platform-api dashboard captures these numbers per surface and per consumer type, and the data was reviewed in the 2026-04-22 platform-api sync. The migration-tracking spreadsheet shows 31 consumers fully on GraphQL and 14 in transition.

Lean toward shipping native iOS and Android apps separately rather than committing to a Flutter rewrite for the next major release. Personally I would rather invest the cycles in better feature parity between the two native codebases than absorb the cost of a unified-but-imperfect Flutter port. My take is that the team's existing native expertise is a real asset and a rewrite would burn it. The team's preference, based on the 2026-Q1 retro, has been consistent here: keep native, improve shared tooling. Recommend we revisit this conversation in a year if the cross-platform tooling landscape changes meaningfully. I would also lean toward investing in a stronger mobile-platform team to absorb shared infra rather than expecting product engineers to maintain it. None of this is committed; the platform-mobile review meets next month and we should have the conversation in detail then.

Team's preference is to consolidate on Kafka for everything because it is already in the stack and the operational expertise is mature. Personally I would lean toward NATS for the smaller event-bus workloads where Kafka is overkill, but I am happy to defer to the team consensus on this one. Recommend we resist the temptation to introduce a third broker for any new workload until we have data showing Kafka does not fit. My take is that the operational simplicity of one broker outweighs the marginal performance gains we might see on small workloads. Lean toward investing in better Kafka client libraries and shared schemas rather than diversifying the stack. I would also argue we should retire the legacy RabbitMQ usage in the few remaining services rather than letting it linger. None of this is committed; the platform-data review covers this in two weeks.

Advocate for sticking with one CDN even though multi-CDN is theoretically better for resilience. Personally I would lean toward investing in better origin-shielding and request coalescing on the single CDN rather than absorbing the operational cost of running multi-CDN. The team's standing position has been consistent here: one CDN, but with strong operational practices around it. Recommend we revisit the conversation if the cost or reliability picture shifts meaningfully. My take is that multi-CDN's marginal benefit on the 99.9th percentile would not justify the contract complexity and the routing-logic burden. Lean toward investing in deep observability of the single-CDN setup before adding diversity. I would also argue against the partial multi-CDN proposal that was floated last quarter; partial is the worst of both worlds.

Prefer keeping session cookies for the web app despite JWT advantages on the mobile and API surfaces. Personally I would lean toward keeping the session-cookie path opaque and server-validated for the web because it is simpler to reason about for the security team. The team's preference, based on the 2026-Q1 review, has been consistent: cookies on web, JWT on mobile and public API. Recommend we resist the periodic temptation to homogenize the auth model. My take is that the developer-experience win of unifying everything on JWT is overstated; the operational risk of token misuse on the web surface is real. Lean toward investing in better cookie rotation and stricter samesite policies rather than migrating. I would also argue we should retire the legacy session-cookie format that some older services still emit.

In favor of consolidating to SES for transactional email and retiring SendGrid even though the migration cost is non-trivial. Personally I would lean toward keeping a small fallback path on SendGrid for the rare provider-outage scenario, but I am open to being convinced. Recommend we run the consolidation in two phases: SES-only for SMB tier first, then enterprise. My take is that the SendGrid reliability has been mixed enough that the operational simplification of consolidating outweighs the safety of dual providers. Lean toward investing in better template-versioning and content-quality tooling on SES before we add new senders. I would also argue we should explicitly carve out customer-research notifications as out-of-scope for the consolidation, since the volume is small and the feature set is different.

Lean toward a hybrid recommender that combines collaborative filtering with the new two-tower retrieval model rather than committing to pure embedding-based recs. Personally I would prefer to keep a strong rule-based fallback for the cold-start funnel because the embedding model is weak there. The team's preference has shifted on this one over the past quarter; the latest stance is hybrid as default with experiments on pure-embedding for specific surfaces. Recommend we resist the urge to chase the latest model architecture before we have a clean A/B framework. My take is that the operational complexity of maintaining the hybrid setup is well within our team's capacity. Lean toward investing in better A/B tooling and feature-store hygiene before adding new model variants. None of this is committed; the recs-platform review covers this next sprint.

My preference is to ship Grafana over the vendor dashboard for SRE workflows even though Datadog's dashboard is more polished. Personally I would lean toward investing in better Grafana templating so the SRE workflow does not feel impoverished. The team's preference, since the dashboards-as-code migration, has been consistent: Grafana for ops, Datadog as the underlying metric store. Recommend we resist the periodic push to standardize back on the vendor UI; the dashboards-as-code workflow has been a real productivity win. My take is that the small ergonomic gap on Grafana is worth the long-term flexibility. Lean toward investing in better alerting integration between Grafana and PagerDuty rather than rebuilding the alert layer. None of this is committed; the platform-ops review meets next month.

Recommend investing in observability before adding more infra capacity. Personally I would lean toward instrumenting the existing fleet thoroughly before we provision additional nodes, because the data so far suggests we are not capacity-bound on aggregate but are bottlenecked on a small set of poorly understood code paths. The team's standing position is similar: observability first, capacity second. My take is that adding capacity without good data is the most expensive way to mask a regression. Lean toward investing in flame-graph capture and continuous profiling on the affected services. I would also argue we should retire two of the legacy node groups that are barely used; the operational tax is real. None of this is committed; the platform-infra review covers it in two weeks.

Would rather scale vertically with managed Postgres than shard ourselves. Personally I would lean toward absorbing the cost of larger Aurora instances for the foreseeable future rather than building and operating our own sharding layer. The team's standing position has been consistent here: avoid sharding until the data clearly does not fit on a single writer. Recommend we resist the periodic enthusiasm for sharding that comes up whenever we hit a performance ceiling. My take is that the operational complexity of sharding outweighs the cost savings on capacity for our scale. Lean toward investing in better query optimization and connection-pool management before changing the topology. I would also argue we should aggressively decommission legacy reader replicas that nobody uses. None of this is committed.

In favor of Temporal-style durable workflows over cron-style scheduling for any new long-running orchestration. Personally I would lean toward keeping cron for the simple periodic jobs that do not need durability semantics; not everything needs the full Temporal stack. The team's preference, based on the 2026-Q1 retro, has been consistent: Temporal for durable, cron for simple. Recommend we resist the urge to migrate every existing cron job to Temporal just because the platform is available; the migration cost is real and the benefit is marginal for many workloads. My take is that we should set explicit guidelines for when each is appropriate. Lean toward investing in better cron-job observability rather than sweeping migrations. None of this is committed; the platform-scheduling review covers it next month.
